policy_title: Implement Strict Fiscal Rules and Strengthen the OBR
stated: Labour will base all government commitments on sound money and economic stability, adhering to fiscal rules that require the current budget to balance and debt to fall as a share of the economy by the fifth year of the forecast. The party will strengthen the Office for Budget Responsibility, ensuring all significant tax or spending changes are subject to its independent forecast, and reject a return to austerity.

source.quote:
Every commitment a Labour government makes will be based on sound money and economic stability. This is a non-negotiable principle for our changed Labour Party. Our fiscal rules are that: 
• The current budget moves into balance, so that day-to-day costs are met by revenues 
• Debt must be falling as a share of the economy by the fifth year of the forecast. There will be no return to austerity. Unlike the Conservatives, Labour will never sideline the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) for political convenience. Instead, we will strengthen the role of the OBR. Every fiscal event making significant changes to taxation or spending will be subject to an independent OBR forecast.

bearing_set.reason: The policy directly targets debt-path sustainability and current-budget balance — the OBR's independent forecast and the two stated fiscal rules (current budget balance; debt falling as % GDP by year 5) bear squarely on whether public finances are funded rather than borrowed, and on the long-run debt burden.

Credible, independently-verified fiscal rules bear on aggregate living standards via a named mechanism: lower sovereign risk premium → reduced gilt yields → lower cost of private investment → productivity and growth; conversely, pro-cyclical rigidity in downturns can widen output gaps — a genuinely contested dual-horizon effect on real living standards.

membership_note: O12 is the designed-for fundamental; O13 earns a real (contested) verdict through the fiscal-credibility-to-investment-cost transmission mechanism. Public-service quality effects (O3/O7/O8) are too composition-dependent to mechanistically assign without knowing the balance between revenue growth and spending paths; O14 is indeterminate for the same reason.
